role: Top-level driver of the rerun: three sessions of parts A, L and C.
purpose: go.sh first checks that the machine and the files are the expected ones. Then it runs three sessions of part A (`ra.sh`), part L and part C (both through `rx.sh`), and one more part C process at the end.

main_flow.step: Set `set -u`, the paths on CRB, the two expected sha256 values and the expected boot id.
Define the helpers `state` (prints one state line) and `fail` (prints the reason and ends the run with exit status 1).
Print the process id of go.sh.
Run the checks: marker file, lock file, sha256 of `rx.sh` and of bwx12, presence of `ra.sh` and the spec files, boot id, MemTotal. Each failed check calls `fail`.
Define `rxok` (tests the `rc` line that `rx.sh` wrote) and `runx` (one call of `rx.sh` with its two checks).
Print the Linux kernel command line, the governors, the huge page settings, the CPU list of the shell and the first state line.
For session 1, 2 and 3: run part A with `ra.sh`, then part L with `like.spec`, then part C with `cfwd.spec` (session 2: `crev.spec`). Print a state line after each step.
Run one more part C process with `crev.spec` (name `T72C4`).
Print the last state line and `ALLDONE`.

behavior_notes: go.sh measures nothing itself. It reads no clock for a rate and computes no rate. All timed intervals are inside the binaries bw_old, bw_new and bwx12. While a binary runs, go.sh only waits for `ra.sh` or `rx.sh`.
A failed check stops the whole run with exit status 1 (function `fail`, line 18). Result folders that were written before the failure stay on disk.
The script does not use `set -e`. A failed command without `|| fail` does not stop the run. Lines 35 to 38 are of this kind.

Order of the 120-thread work: part A, part L, part C, then part A of the next session. The last process of part A is bw_old with the kernel `read` [Ref2]. The part L process starts after it, and its first kernel is `oldread` [Ref4].

Gap before each bwx12 process: in the rerun each of the 7 launch lines is 5 s after the time in the name of its result folder [Ref8]. One 1 s sleep of the wait loop would give 6 s or more. So the wait for at most 2 runnable tasks ended at its first test each time.
CPU list: go.sh sets no CPU list. `ra.sh` restarts itself under `taskset -c 0-119` [Ref2]. `rx.sh` starts the binary under `taskset -c 0-119` [Ref3].

How go.sh was started on CRB: no script of the run folder holds the command. An AI agent (Claude Code) ran the rerun. Its transcript (the saved record of its commands and their outputs) holds the command [Ref12]. The agent sent one command line from its server to CRB with `ssh` (the remote login tool), as the user `jhan`. The part that starts go.sh reads: `L=~/cache-perf/results/go-T72-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).log; nohup setsid ~/cache-perf/w120-7200-20261117/go.sh > $L 2>&1 < /dev/null &`.

What the start command sets: `> $L 2>&1` sends the standard output and the error output of go.sh to the log file [Ref1]. go.sh itself names no log file. `< /dev/null` gives go.sh an empty input. `nohup` starts go.sh with the hangup signal ignored. The hangup signal tells a program that its terminal or connection was closed. `setsid` makes go.sh the leader of a new process group [Ref13]. So the `kill` command that line 19 prints reaches go.sh and its child processes.

The start command holds no `taskset` [Ref12]. So it did not set the CPU list `0-119` that line 38 printed. The shell of go.sh got this list from the process that started it [Ref11]. An inspection of CRB on 2026-10-30 found the systemd setting `CPUAffinity=0-119` [Ref14]. systemd is the first process of the system. The setting gives this list to systemd and to every process that descends from it. The scripts of the rerun do not read this setting. On the day of the rerun the agent ran `taskset -cp $$` on CRB through `ssh`, about 5 s before the start command. It printed the list `0-119` for the shell that ran this command [Ref15].

Is the local go.sh the script that ran: yes, except for the message of line 20. The next note gives the difference. The log of go.sh and the files that the run wrote to its result folders hold no checksum of go.sh. The transcript holds the command that copied the files to CRB [Ref15]. The agent wrote the sha256 of go.sh, `ra.sh` and the three spec files to the file `local.sha` on its server. It copied the five files and `local.sha` to CRB. There `sha256sum -c local.sha` printed `OK` for each of the five files, about 5 s before the start command. The transcript holds no command of the agent between this test and the start command. On 2026-11-21 the local go.sh still had the sha256 that `local.sha` lists for it (tested with `sha256sum -c`) [Ref16].

Two texts of go.sh: the local text differs from the text that ran in line 20 only. On 2026-11-24 the message of that line was changed on the instruction of the user of the AI agent [Ref18]. The old line was `[ -e /tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING ] && fail "RUNNING file present"`. With the old line put back, the local go.sh has the sha256 that `local.sha` lists for it [Ref20]. The transcript of the rerun holds the last command that wrote go.sh before the copy to CRB. The script text in that command has the same sha256 [Ref15].

Effect of the edit on two checks: `local.sha` was not changed. So `sha256sum -c local.sha` now prints `go.sh: FAILED` and `OK` for the 4 other files [Ref16]. The script `build_facts.py` builds the facts sheet of the rerun (the file `FACTS.md` in this folder). Its check 20 makes the same test as `sha256sum -c` [Ref19]. So a new run of `build_facts.py` fails this check. It then stops and writes no file. With the old line put back it passes [Ref20].
The copy of go.sh on CRB: the edit was made in the local file only. Insufficient data: the present text of the copy on CRB. `sha256sum go.sh` on CRB would resolve it.

What `users` in a state line shows: the number of lines that `who` prints. After the start of go.sh the start command waited on CRB for the end of go.sh (`wait $pid`). Then it printed the exit status and the log [Ref12]. So the `ssh` connection of the start command was open during the whole run. All 12 state lines show `users 0` [Ref1]. So `who` did not list this connection. `users 0` does not show that no connection to CRB was open.

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the whole-chip read test of 2026-11-17, run after the memory speed was lowered from 8000 MT/s to 7200 MT/s.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed.
one DIMM. CRB has 12 slots.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.
a process is one start of a benchmark binary.
one pass of go.sh through part A, part L and part C.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
a text file that `rx.sh` reads as its input. Each line is `tag|arguments of the binary` and gives one process. The tag becomes the name of the csv file of that process.
a text file whose lines hold values separated by commas.
a line that go.sh or go2.sh prints with the time, the boot id, MemTotal, the load, the logins and the processes per user.
the stop rule of bandwidth.c: after the minimum time (0.5 s here) each thread finishes the pass over its buffer that it is in. The threads stop at different times.
the stop rule used with bwx12 here: all threads stop at the same time (after 6 s).

the file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`. The scripts of this test stop when it exists. Since 2026-11-24 the message of go.sh line 20 says what the file stands for: Jeremy or someone else is using CRB. The messages of `ra.sh`, `rx.sh` and go2.sh do not say it. None of the scripts that test the file says who creates it. The facts sheet of the rerun says that another user creates it during a performance test [Ref10].

another user of CRB. A block is a time window in which the whole machine is reserved for the measurements of Jeremy. Notes of 2026-10-30 say that the marker file is present for the whole of each block [Ref17].
a random identifier that Linux creates at each start. Equal boot ids mean the same boot.
the usable memory that Linux reports, in kB.

the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes (file `/proc/loadavg`). The fourth field of the file gives the tasks that are runnable now and the number of all tasks, for example `1/1013` [Ref9].
the number before the slash in the fourth field of `/proc/loadavg`: the processes and threads that are runnable at the moment of the reading [Ref9].
the Linux policy that sets the CPU frequency.
a Linux feature that can place a buffer on 2 MiB pages. The two files that line 37 prints hold its settings.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.
the number that a process returns when it ends. 0 means success. `launches.txt` writes it as `rc`.

`launches.txt` is a file that `rx.sh` writes in each of its result folders. `rx.sh` appends a `launch` line directly before it starts a process: the tag, the time, the content of `/proc/loadavg`, the number of logins and the arguments. It appends an `rc` line after the process has ended: the exit status, the tag and the time.
the number that Linux gives to a process.
a set of processes that one signal can reach together. The group has the process id of its leader as its number.
the number under which a process holds an open file.
the CPUs on which Linux may run a process (its CPU affinity). A child process starts with the list of its parent [Ref11].
a Linux tool. `taskset -c 0-119 COMMAND` starts a command that may run on the CPUs 0 to 119 only. `taskset -cp PID` prints the CPU list of a running process.
the command line that started go.sh on CRB. It is not part of a script. An AI agent (Claude Code) ran the rerun, and the saved record of its commands holds this command line [Ref12].
Coordinated Universal Time. All times of the run are written in UTC.

functions.name: state
functions.what: Prints one state line: label, time, boot id, MemTotal, load, logins, marker file, processes per user.

functions.name: fail
functions.what: Prints `FAILED:` and the message, prints a state line, ends go.sh with exit status 1.

functions.name: rxok
functions.what: Tests that `launches.txt` of the newest result folder of that name holds exactly one `rc` line, with status 0.

functions.name: runx
functions.what: Runs `rx.sh` with one spec file. Stops the run when `rx.sh` or bwx12 failed. Prints a state line.
